topic: Algebra III - Permutations & Combinations, Matrices & Determinants

sections.title: Fundamental Principle of Counting
sections.content: If an event can occur in 'm' different ways and another event can occur in 'n' different ways, then both events can occur in 'm × n' ways (Multiplication Rule: AND). If either one or the other can occur, it's 'm + n' ways (Addition Rule: OR).

sections.title: Permutations (Arrangements)
sections.content: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a specific order. The number of permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is nPr = n! / (n-r)!. Order strictly matters here.

sections.title: Combinations (Selections)
sections.content: A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter. The number of combinations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is nCr = n! / [r!(n-r)!].

sections.title: Introduction to Matrices
sections.content: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Important types include Row matrix, Column matrix, Square matrix (rows = columns), Diagonal matrix, Identity matrix (I), and Null matrix (O).

sections.title: Matrix Operations
sections.content: Addition and Subtraction require matrices of the same order. Matrix Multiplication (A × B) requires the number of columns in A to equal the number of rows in B. It is calculated by multiplying rows of A with columns of B (Row-by-Column).

sections.title: Determinants (2x2 and 3x3)
sections.content: A determinant is a scalar value associated with a square matrix. For a 2x2 matrix [a b; c d], det = ad - bc. For 3x3, expand along any row or column using the alternating signs (+ - +).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Using nPr instead of nCr when order doesn't matter (like choosing a committee).
2) Assuming Matrix Multiplication is commutative (AB is NOT always equal to BA).
3) Messing up the negative sign for the middle term when expanding a 3x3 determinant.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 1 covers counting basic arrangements (nPr) and selections (nCr). It introduces matrices as arrays with specific multiplication rules, and determinants as their numerical counterparts.

tricks.title: Combination Symmetry Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Selecting 'r' objects is exactly the same as rejecting 'n-r' objects.
tricks.example: nCr = nC(n-r). For example, 10C8 is exactly equal to 10C2 = 10*9 / 2*1 = 45.

tricks.title: Diagonals of a Polygon
tricks.explanation: Use a direct combination formula to find the number of diagonals in an n-sided polygon.
tricks.example: Diagonals = nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2. For a hexagon (n=6), 6(3)/2 = 9 diagonals.

tricks.title: Factorial Basics
tricks.explanation: Memorize the base cases for factorials to speed up calculations.

tricks.title: Matrix Multiplication Identity
tricks.explanation: Multiplying any matrix by the Identity Matrix leaves it unchanged.

tricks.title: Sarrus Rule for 3x3 Determinant
tricks.explanation: A quick visual trick to solve 3x3 determinants without expanding: write the first two columns again, add products of primary diagonals, and subtract products of secondary diagonals.

tricks.title: Consecutive Combinations Addition
tricks.explanation: Adding two combinations with the same 'n' and consecutive 'r' values increases 'n' by 1.
